loader_evidence_only_not_a_serving_path.conclusion: With max_length raised to 4096 the loader encodes all 2049 tokens (no truncation). With max_length=2048 it silently drops the last token (kept 2048 of 2049), raises nothing and prints nothing, and returns a valid unit-norm 2048-d vector that differs from the full-input vector (cosine 0.999981). The loader's own truncation is therefore not a usable limit signal; the Foundry-side count-and-refuse check is required.

meaning_for_inputs_at_or_below_2048_toke: The warning is about a key that is simply not part of the YaRN schema; it is not a failure and MLX never consults it.

MLX applies YaRN (factor 16, original 16384) to all positions: 27 of 64 rotary frequency pairs are slowed by 16x and 16 partially, at every sequence length including <=2048; the yarn magnitude scale is 1.0.
llama_4 position scaling 1 + 0.1*ln(1+floor(pos/16384)) is exactly 1.0 for every position below 16384, so it is a no-op at <=2048 and also at 2049.

Whether the upstream model wants YaRN applied (apply_yarn_scaling=false could mean 'disabled' in NeMo) is NOT resolved offline. Sensitivity: swapping YaRN for plain RoPE (same unchanged loader, only the rope constructor swapped) moves the vector by cosine 1.0000 (10 tok), 0.9996 (330 tok), 0.9986 (1024 tok), 0.9971 (2048 tok).
That is a small but non-zero length-dependent shift; the torch/sentence-transformers reference (needs authorization) is what would settle which side matches upstream. No quality claim.

g_admission.design: worker threads call the unchanged loader through PyO3. A = long 2048-token encode, abandoned 100 ms after it starts (the client 'times out' and stops waiting; there is no cancel API). B = a short query arriving right after. Scenario 1 adds nothing; scenario 2 holds an atomic busy slot in the worker thread itself until the encode returns.
findings: Timed-out call keeps running: A finished 887 / 1589 ms after the simulated client timeout (run 1 / run 2); nothing cancels it.

Calls are not serialized: B entered Python 0.1 ms after it was requested while A was still executing, and both ran (A and B finished 167 / 37 ms apart in runs 1 / 2, B first). B completed 721 / 1552 ms after its request vs 35 / 103 ms solo, so its latency was set by A's remaining work on the shared GPU queue; against the 1500 ms query ceiling that is over it in 1 of 2 runs (721 ms / 1552 ms). [inference] A does not hold the GIL for its whole call (MLX evaluation releases it).

Neither the loader nor PyO3 exposes a queue limit, busy refusal or cancellation. One active request with no queue therefore has to be enforced by worker-owned state: scenario 2's worker-held slot refused B at 0 ms before any work and stayed held until A truly finished (848 / 1418 ms after the client gave up).

A client-side semaphore alone would have released at the timeout while A kept executing for another 887 / 1589 ms (runs 1 / 2). Stopping abandoned work needs process termination, which this scratch run did not exercise.
g_admission.scope: evidence for the later supervisor; the atomic slot is scratch bridge code, not a product mechanism
